19776-the-ordeal-a-mountain-romance-of-t:
Charles Egbert Craddock was the pen name of Mary Noailles Murfree. The Ordeal is her mountain romance of Tennessee. It opens in the Great Smoky Mountains after the springs hotel has closed. The Briscoe family lingers too long at their summer cottage, neighbors think. The hotel guests and staff have all vanished townward. Solitude there turns sharp enough to foster fear.

Murfree made the Tennessee mountains famous in fiction. Her dialect and scenery set the standard for Appalachian local color. Isolation drives her plots: weather, kin, and old feuds close in. The Ordeal works that pattern in romance form. Readers get the Smokies before the national park existed. Her mountains are wilder and lonelier than today's.
20091-no-surrender-a-tale-of-the-rising-:
G. A. Henty wrote No Surrender, a tale of the rising in La Vendée, in France. The Vendée rose against the French Revolution in a fierce civil war. Thick woods, called the Bocage, covered much of that region. Such ground should have helped local fighters who knew each lane.

Yet, Henty notes, the rebels fought most big battles in open ground. There, trained troops held the edge over brave but raw bands. His tale follows young heroes caught in that doomed, brave rising. Readers get Henty's blend of true war history and boys' adventure at full stretch.
20449-the-plum-tree:
David Graham Phillips published The Plum Tree in 1905, a novel about the spoils of American politics. In the slang of the time, plums were the jobs and favors a winning party handed out. The story follows a man drawn into that system of power.

The narrator recalls his young wife at their scant breakfast table. He was as blue as ever a man of twenty-five could be, while she stayed brave and confident. Her courage, he says, was no pretense meant to cheer him. Phillips builds his tale of ambition and corruption on such home scenes.
20628-torchy-and-vee:
Sewell Ford's Torchy and Vee, published in 1918, marries off his red-headed office hero at last. Vee is the stenographer Torchy courted through the earlier books. Now they keep house together, and Torchy narrates married life in his unstoppable slang.

He looks forward to enjoying a little family reunion. Vee will tell him how she has been getting along, and what cute tricks young Master Richard has developed while he was gone. But right in the midst of the domestic sketch, Vee breaks loose with news of her own. Ford keeps the office comedy running at home.
20909-under-the-tree:
A shadow slips across the ground, and a child looks up to the sky in Under the Tree. It hangs on the poplar, jerks, then creeps away and will not stay. Elizabeth Madox Roberts writes as if some chain pulls it from the top.

Roberts's 1922 poems catch the world as a small child sees and names it. Trees, clouds, and beasts take on fresh, strange life in her lines. She wrote from Kentucky with a child's eye and a poet's ear, in a small classic of childhood verse. The book is a small book of verse for the young.
21051-skylark-three:
Liberties with sound science are owned up front in Skylark Three, with a frank caveat. Some theories used here its author holds sound, some unsound, and some beyond his line. E. E. Smith asks readers to grant that mix as the tale's base.

Richard Seaton and his crew ride the vast Skylark Three among alien worlds. Fenachrone foes, space fleets, and wonders of scale fill Smith's sequel. His Lensman-age craft of piling marvel on marvel runs at full tilt here. Readers who crave old, huge space opera will find Skylark Three a rich, breathless feast of it.
21103-sisters-three:
Norah, Lettice, and Hilary are sisters growing up in England's Lake District, daughters of a well-known author. Mrs George de Horne Vaizey opens on New Year's Day, with the girls sighing for something nice to happen amid practising, housework, and classes. Change comes when one sister reaches marriageable age.

She chooses among eligible young men, and the wedding plans advance a long way. Then she realises she cannot go through with it. Around that crisis Vaizey draws daily life for young women around 1900, down to judging young men by their moustaches. The tale stays light even when hearts are at stake.
21883-we-three:
A man plans his winters around a woman he must not meet in Gouverneur Morris's We Three, published in 1916. If Lucy Fulton goes to Palm Beach, he will go to Aiken; if she goes to Newport, he will take Bar Harbor. They have been asked not to meet, he says, and will do so only by accident. Then he starts again at the beginning, with a small boy warned against matches.

That boy played with matches anyway and never burned anything down, which is his parable for the tale. Morris builds a society romance on restraint: two people, a promise, and a third life between them. Henry Hutt's pictures show Lucy dark against a lit hall. The voice is dry, rueful, and very much of its wealthy world.
21934-the-gold-of-fairnilee:
Fairy gold glitters under a Scottish Border house in Andrew Lang's The Gold of Fairnilee. Lang made the tale for a child far away in Australia. Lang tells his niece Jeanie that he and her father dug for treasure as boys in the Camp of Rink, and found none. The story, he promises, will tell her why. Randal of Fairnilee lives three hundred sixty years before the reader, in a high house with pepperbox towers.

His father is gone to the wars, and Randal lives with his mother, old nurse Nancy, and Simon Grieve the butler. Fairies, a hidden hoard, and the Flodden sorrow of Scotland weave through the tale. Lang mixes history and fairy lore in his tenderest manner. It is his own favorite among his tales for children.
21956-report-of-the-knaresbrough-rail-wa:
A canal that became a railway is argued for in this 1820 report of the Knaresborough Rail-Way Committee in Yorkshire. In March 1818 the town's meeting authorized a survey for the most eligible line, at first for a canal. The report addresses the noblemen, gentlemen, and subscribers on the adopted line with due deference. The Nidd valley, it notes, turns sixty-seven mills with its falls.

The committee pleads that hostile landlords, poor soil, or weak trade might once have killed the project, but none of these now applies. Knaresborough's slow progress beside other towns is held up as the shame to cure. The pamphlet is a fossil of the railway age's birth: local pride, water power, and a surveyor's line offered to an enlightened and liberal public.
22236-flag-of-the-free:
Flag of the Free is a slim volume of patriotic verse published in 1917, the year America entered the Great War. Its title poem addresses the flag directly. Bright beacon of the azure sky, the poet calls it, true light of freedom's dome. The poem prays that the flag will shine until all nations cease to grope in vain for liberty.

Such verse flooded American print in 1917 and 1918. Schools, newspapers, and war meetings all wanted poems that schoolchildren could recite and crowds could cheer. Flag of the Free is a surviving sample of that home-front poetry. It shows how the flag's cult looked in print at the moment of America's first great crusade abroad.
22354-the-adventures-of-maya-the-bee:
Waldemar Bonsels wrote The Adventures of Maya the Bee, published in English in 1922. Maya is a baby bee waking to life in the hive. An elderly lady-bee named Cassandra helps her slip from her cell.

Cassandra commands great respect among the bees. Those were exciting days in the bee nation, Bonsels writes. A rebellion had broken out that the queen could not suppress. Maya thus enters a hive already in turmoil and change. Her adventures carry young readers through the insect world. The story mixes nature lore with a small heroine's curiosity. It became a lasting favorite of children's literature in many lands.
a-master-s-degree:
Margaret Hill McCarter dedicates her novel to the Kansas boys and girls who have not yet earned their degrees. The story begins at Sunrise College. Professor Vincent Burgess of Boston arrives there to teach Greek. On the same September day, Vic Burleigh enrolls as a freshman. Burleigh is a big country boy from beyond the Walnut River.

Fifteen chapters follow college games, storms, a stolen silver pitcher, and the troubles of students and teachers on the Kansas prairie. Burgess and Burleigh grow through loss, duty, and hard choices. McCarter writes a wholesome campus tale about education as character, aimed at young readers of her day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acanthus-titu:
Acanthus, a Macedonian titular see on the Strymonic Gulf, is now Erisso. Herodotus, book seven, records Xerxes praising its inhabitants for their zeal in his cause. That classical praise gives the small see a place in Greek history well before its Christian record.

The ruins of a large curving mole jutting far into the sea still stood in the early nineteenth century. The entry cites Smith's dictionary of Greek and Roman geography and Leake's travels in northern Greece, and its brevity matches a see known chiefly by site, ancient praise, and surviving harbour works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-augus:
Antoine-Augustin Touttée, a French Benedictine monk of the Maurist reform, lived from 1677 to 1718. After study with the Oratorians at Riom, he took vows at Vendôme and taught philosophy and theology at three abbeys. He then withdrew to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris to prepare a new edition of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem.

His Greek text with a Latin translation appeared after his death in 1720, edited by Prudent Maran. Three learned essays on Cyril's life, writings, and teaching open the volume. At the time it stood as the standard edition, and the entry presents Touttée as a quiet scholar whose one great book outlived him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bersabee:
Bersabee, or Beersheba, a town at Palestine's southern edge, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Through most of Hebrew history it marked the south as Dan marked the north, so that from Dan to Bersabee meant the whole land. After the northern kingdom's fall, the phrase shifted to other southern bounds.

Its name draws long debate, with wells, oaths, and seven sacred things all proposed, and two Genesis stories giving rival accounts of its naming by Abraham and Isaac. The entry weighs Hebrew roots, wells, and patriarchal tales. It is a place-name study as much as a town history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold-of-c:
Berthold of Chiemsee, a German bishop and theological writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His true name was Berthold Pürstinger, born at Salzburg in 1465 and dead at Saalfelden in 1543. Trained in civil and church law, he served as master of the chamber to Salzburg's archbishop and became Bishop of Chiemsee in 1508.

Residing at Salzburg as coadjutor to the archbishop, he wrote against the Lutheran reform, defending Catholic teaching in clear German prose. He resigned his see in 1525 and spent his last years writing. The entry presents a bishop-scholar answering the Reformation from within the old Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cedar-tree:
The cedar tree of the Bible, Hebrew érez, Greek kedros, Latin cedrus, usually means the celebrated cedar of Lebanon. The name can cover several conifers, but in most passages the Lebanon cedar is meant. It is a tree of high stature, raised high above every other tree in the land, as Ezekiel and Isaiah describe it. Its wood and its height made it a natural image of majesty.

In a few passages, though, the Lebanon cedar cannot be meant. In Leviticus and Numbers the wood had to be one the Israelites could readily find during their desert wandering. A juniper of the Arabah, Juniperus Phoenicea, whose wood is also aromatic, is the likelier tree. The article weighs each passage in turn to decide which tree the text intends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-miche:
An entry on Charles Michel de l'Epée, the French priest who invented a sign alphabet for teaching deaf people and founded their schooling. Born at Versailles in 1712, he studied theology but was refused ordination for declining to condemn Jansenism. After qualifying in law, he was ordained by the Bishop of Troyes and returned to Paris, where he took on the education of two deaf sisters.

De l'Epée built a set of conventional signs into a full alphabet, teaching through the eye what hearing children learn through the ear. He opened a school at his own expense and outdid earlier teachers such as Pereira, Bulwer, and Wallis. His method was later replaced by lip-reading, in which pupils watch and copy lip and tongue movements. The entry credits his sign system with laying the foundations of organised instruction of the deaf. He died in Paris in 1789.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-van:
Gregory Cleary's entry treats Cornelius van Zierikzee, born at Zierikzee, a Zeeland town in Holland, about 1405, died 21 February 1462. The Franciscan Rule's strict observance, upheld and propagated through Italy by Saint Bernardine of Siena and Saint John Capistran, had early entered Germany. At twenty Cornelius entered the Franciscan Order in Cologne province, then including most of the Netherlands. That province was famous for its members' number and sanctity, including several Scotsmen educated at Continental universities.

Bernardine's revival of Franciscan life no doubt reached King James I of Scotland, whose poetic spirit harmonized with the Franciscan ideal. In 1436 the king asked the order's superiors for Friars of the Observance to be sent into Scotland. The Scottish Franciscans enjoyed a great European reputation for adhering most conscientiously and strictly to the order's poverty and austerity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cree:
An ethnological entry introduces the Cree, the greatest and most important Indian tribe of Canada, part of the great Algonquin stock and close kin to the Ojibwa. Before confinement to reservations, their bands held vast territory around Lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba and the lower Red and Saskatchewan rivers, and east toward Hudson Bay.

Known to Jesuit missionaries about 1650, the Cree pushed onto the open plains once English trading posts supplied firearms, driving the Blackfeet before them and warring with the Tinneh tribes. A smallpox epidemic in 1781 cut their numbers sharply. The entry covers their alliances, wars, physique, and customs, and notes their generally friendly relations with both French and English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-decree:
A canon law entry defines a decree, from Latin for I judge, as an order or law made by superior authority for others' direction. In church use it takes several senses. Any papal Bull, Brief, or Motu Proprio counts as a decree, as a legislative act of the Holy Father. Pope Siricius already cites the general decrees of Liberius.

Roman Congregations issue decrees within their jurisdiction, and provinces and dioceses issue them in synods. The word also names collections of church law, above all Gratian's Decree. Papal and council decrees bind universally, while Trent first applied the term indiscriminately to rulings on faith and reform. Congregation decrees bind certainly in the case judged, but whether they bind as general law depends on whether they enlarge or merely explain the law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-edou:
Francois Edouard Joachim Coppee, born at Paris on 26 January 1842 and dead on 23 May 1908, was a French poet, dramatist, and novelist of the Parnassian school. His father, a War Department clerk, modelled a true Christian life. Francois studied at Lycee Saint-Louis until straitened family means forced him out before graduating to help support them. He finished his education by private study in long hours at the Sainte-Genevieve Library after hard days' work.

Joining the Parnassian poets in 1863, he published his first verses, Le Reliquaire, in 1866, followed by Intimites, and his first play, Le Passant, in 1869. Through Princesse Mathilde he became assistant librarian of the Senate, then librarian of the Comedie Francaise from 1871 to 1885. He won the Legion of Honour in 1876 and entered the French Academy in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Spee, a Jesuit poet born on the Rhine in 1591, wrote the book that first broke the witch trials in Germany. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1610, taught at Trier, Würzburg, and other cities, and was ordained in 1622. An attempt on his life at Peine in 1629 failed. He died at Trier in 1635 from sickness caught while nursing the suffering in a hospital.

His Cautio Criminalis, printed without his name in 1631, laid bare the rack, the forced confessions, and the unjust judges of the trials. Spee sought reform rather than instant abolition, yet his book ended witch burning at Mainz and pointed the way to its slow end elsewhere. His sacred songs, the Trutznachtigall, still rank high among seventeenth-century religious lyrics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-augus:
Gabriel-Auguste Daubrée, a French geologist born at Metz in 1814, founded experimental geology by making rocks in the laboratory. Trained in mining engineering at the École Polytechnique, he entered government service in 1834 and published on Scandinavian ore deposits, winning the notice of Berzelius. A Strasburg chair from 1849 gave him the laboratory his experiments needed.

Daubrée made minerals by art, tested superheated steam, grinding, pressure, and strain in mountain building, and studied the hot springs of Plombières in detail. Admitted to the Academy of Sciences in 1861, he taught geology at Paris's Natural History Museum and later directed the School of Mines. A mineral in meteoric iron, daubréelite, still bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galilee:
Galilee, the native land of Jesus, is where he began his ministry, worked many wonders, and chose his apostles. The Hebrew name comes from a word for circle or district, first marking the part of Naphtali around Kedesh, a city of refuge. Solomon's gift of twenty northern towns to Hiram of Tyre also bore the name, and Isaiah called the mixed land Galilee of the Nations.

By New Testament times Galilee, with Samaria and Judea, divided western Palestine, split by a ridge into Upper and Lower halves. Josephus counted 204 thriving villages and fifteen walled towns there, on soil rich enough for a great people. Today its folk are few and scattered, though Safed in the north and Nazareth in the south still anchor the old land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-de-la:
Gilbert de la Porrée, also called Gilbertus Porretanus, was a philosopher, theologian, and Bishop of Poitiers, born at Poitiers in 1076 and dead in 1154. He studied under Hilary at Poitiers, Bernard at Chartres, and Anselm at Laon, where he likely first met Abelard. He taught philosophy at Chartres for about fifteen years before becoming a bishop in 1142. A Catholic Encyclopedia article places him at the heart of early scholastic thought.

His Liber Sex Principiorum explained Aristotle's last six categories and served as a school textbook for three centuries. His commentary on Boethius on the Trinity drew fire for its doctrine of universals, and two archdeacons carried the charge to Eugene III. St. Bernard opposed him at Paris in 1147 and Reims in 1148, yet the dispute ended without a firm verdict. Later readers have read his realism in several ways, from ontological to moderate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-klee:
Rhineland theologian Heinrich Klee, born at Münstermaifeld in 1800, carried sound Catholic doctrine into rationalist Bonn and on to Möhler's chair at Munich, dying within a year of the move. A Mainz seminarian at seventeen, professor of exegesis and history there in 1824, he took Bonn's chair in 1829 over Freiburg's, facing Hermesian dominance with tact, genial lectures, and learned books.

Ten years at Bonn teaching dogmatic and moral theology, history of dogma, and exegesis won him influence. Munich called him in 1839 after the Cologne archbishop's clash with the Hermesians. His Catholic Dogmatics in three volumes ran through four editions, his history of dogma in two. Commentaries on John, Romans, and Hebrews preceded a posthumous ethics, though views on the soul's origin and unbaptized infants drew criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-and-jul:
Belgian brothers Henri and Jules Desclée founded a monastery and a printing house that reshaped Catholic art and chant. When Kulturkampf exiles from Beuron sought refuge in Belgium, the brothers, Jules a former papal Zouave captain, gave them a Namur estate. There Baron Béthune built Maredsous in pure thirteenth-century Gothic, its 120 monks devoted to liturgy, study, and teaching.

A college and technical school followed in 1882 and 1902, and in 1882 the brothers founded at Tournai the Society of St. John the Evangelist to restore medieval beauty to liturgical books, using English craftsmen at first. Their plainchant editions, following Pothier and Solesmes, grounded the Vatican edition Pius X imposed, and a sister Society of St. Augustine spread the same art to religious books and images.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-see:
The Holy See, from the Latin Sancta Sedes or Holy Chair, takes its name from Rome's bishops' enthronement ceremony. It must not be confused with the ancient gestatorial chair in St. Peter's apse, venerated as the Chair of Peter. In general use it means the supreme pastor of the church's actual seat, or residence, plus the authorities forming the central administration.

In canonical and diplomatic use it matches Apostolic See, Holy Apostolic See, Roman Church, and Roman Curia. The word sedes, chair, first marked churches founded by apostles, then the great patriarchal sees: Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Constantinople. Rome was expressly called the first see properly so named, and the entry traces the title from those roots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-year-of-:
The Holy Year of Jubilee takes its name most probably from the Hebrew jobel, a ram's horn blown to proclaim the celebration. Through Greek and Latin forms the word blended with jubilo, to shout, giving the forms jubilatio and jubilaeum used across Europe. The idea of rejoicing thus clings to the word from its roots.

For Israelites the jubilee was a year of remission and universal pardon. Leviticus commands sanctifying the fiftieth year and proclaiming remission to all inhabitants of the land. Every seventh year was holy for rest, but the year after seven cycles carried special solemnity. Talmudists later disputed whether the jubilee fell in the forty-ninth or fiftieth year, since the latter would set two sabbatical years in a row.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metropolis-ti: This 1913 reference article on Metropolis — the titular see. Siméon Vailhé traces its fragmentary past. Prelates once shepherded the local faithful. Scant records preserve its story. Rome now lists it among titular sees. Its forgotten prelates are famed. Its titular status is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milwaukee: This 1913 reference piece on Milwaukee — the Wisconsin archdiocese. Joseph Rainer gives its founding story. Its archbishops guard the lakeside flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the American north. Its 1843 founding is famed. Its archbishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osee: Hosea was the prophet commanded to marry an unfaithful wife, the living parable of God's love for faithless Israel. This entry examines his book, his marriage, and his message. The prophet of the wounded heart: his children bore names of judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petitions-to-: Petitions to the Holy See are the formal requests by which the faithful seek graces from Rome. This entry explains their kinds, their procedure, and their law. The road from the diocese to the pope: the entry maps its every step.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scillium-titu: Scillium, the Numidian town of the martyrs, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Africa: its twelve martyrs crowned the 180s in Africa's Numidia in the persecution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sea-of-galile: The Sea of Galilee is the lake of the Gospels. This entry covers its shores, its towns, and its sacred history. The waters of the miraculous draught: their holy shores saw the Christ in the 30s A.D. of the Gospels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aengus-the: St. Aengus the Culdee was the poet of the Félire. This entry traces his calendar, his Tallaght, and his fame. The hagiographer of the Irish saints: his famed Félire filled Tallaght in the 800s' Ireland in the monastery of the south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tegernsee: Tegernsee was the abbey of Bavaria. This entry traces its lake, its monks, and its fame. The house of the Alpine shore: its old abbey crowned Tegernsee in the 740s' lake in the Alps of the truly very old south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tennessee: Tennessee is the diocese of the South. This entry traces its Nashville, its parishes, and its churches. The bishopric of the Volunteer State: its new see crowned Nashville in the 1830s' Cumberland in the river of the very old south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-apostolic: The Apostolic See is the throne of Peter. This long entry examines its Rome, its primacy, and its history. The chair of the fisherman: its ancient keys crowned Rome in the 100s of the martyrs in the very old catacombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-d-arcy: McGee was the father of the Canadian confederation. This long entry examines his 1800s, his Montreal, and his murder. The Irish statesman of the Dominion: his proud Montreal crowned Canada in the 1860s of the Fenians in the old city.
doe-osti-3003211-support-for-the-32-sup-: The photochemical society got its meeting support, and this DOE text covers the 32nd annual. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their record. The society was Inter-American. The record was chemist. The annual was 32nd. The society was photochemical.
doe-osti-3015204-support-for-the-30-sup-: Photochemical society got meeting-supported, and this DOE text covers the 30th annual. The pages detail the Inter-American findings. The chemists get their record. The meeting was 30th. The record was chemist. The society was photochemical. The annual was 30th.
doe-osti-3015642-integrated-direct-air-c: DAC got H2-free valorized, and this DOE text captures air carbon without hydrogen. The pages detail the integrated findings. The climate folks get their method. The capture was direct air. The method was climate. The valorization was CO2. The capture was integrated.
doe-osti-3028321-final-report-for-closin: EGS fractures got stress-looped, and this DOE final closes in-situ complexity. The pages detail the report findings. The geothermal folks get their closeout. The complexity was fracture. The closeout was geothermal. The situ were in. The EGS were stress.
doe-osti-3030823-supporting-resource-ade: ReEDS-India got adequacy-supported, and this DOE slides model resource adequacy. The pages detail the findings. The energy folks get their deck. The model was ReEDS-India. The deck was energy. The India were ReEDS. The deck were energy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DiesCommittee_D: nsia-DiesCommittee Dies Committee: the made public government document on the Dies Committee, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DiesSubcommitte:
On June 22, 1944, members of the U.S. House of Representatives debated the work of the Dies Committee on the House floor. An excerpt from the Congressional Record preserves that discussion. The committee, chaired by Martin Dies, was then investigating alleged un-American activity inside the United States.

Floor debates show a committee fighting for its standing in real time. Supporters and critics spoke for the record while the panel's funding and methods were contested in Congress itself. For readers, the excerpt is a direct sample of how the Dies Committee was argued about by the lawmakers who created it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ParmanWalterLee: Walter Lee Parman is named in the title of this declassified US government document, archived by the Internet Archive. The record carries no year, no issuing body, no abstract. Public text not found. It waits here as a name and a file number.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: The Pike Committee was the House of Representatives' 1975 investigation into American intelligence, the partner to the Senate's Church Committee. Its clashes with the Ford White House over access and publication became a story in themselves. This briefing-book page presents the record of that three-way fight among the White House, the CIA, and the committee. The evidence here is the title alone. The subject still matters, because the Pike fight set lasting precedents for how much Congress may see of secret operations.
immensee:
Theodor Storm's Immensee is a short German tale, here translated by C. W. Bell, about memory, youth and a love that time has altered. The edition belongs to a series meant to help English readers meet foreign literature without a bulky dictionary, pairing literary worth with useful vocabulary.

Storm tells his story in the quiet, reflective manner that made his name, letting an older man's return to familiar places stir the scenes of his youth. The lake and woods of the title give the tale its still centre, and Bell's translation aims to join readable English style with strict faithfulness to Storm's German. Readers new to German fiction will find Immensee a gentle, brief introduction to one of its most loved storytellers.
in-the-year-of-jubilee:
George Gissing opens In the Year of Jubilee on a Sunday morning in Camberwell, a respectable suburb of London. Arthur Peachey slips away for his first holiday since his marriage. His wife Ada keeps a showy, slovenly house in De Crespigny Park. Her friends the French sisters, sharp Beatrice and flighty Fanny, fill the rooms with talk.

Gissing follows these young women as they chafe against dull homes and narrow prospects. Courtships, advertisements, and schemes for advancement drive the plot forward. The jubilee year of Queen Victoria gives the book its backdrop of public cheer. Beneath the comedy runs a hard look at marriage, money, and female ambition. Few Victorian novelists watched suburban life with a colder or funnier eye than Gissing shows here.
jack-harkaway-and-his-son-s-escape-from-:
Bracebridge Hemyng's Jack Harkaway and His Son's Escape from the Brigands of Greece continues the Harkaways' Greek adventures. The book opens with a scolding: Mrs. Harkaway's maid, long on an errand, returns with twenty excuses, none of them true.

She has been detained by the Contessa Maraviglia, whose letter invites the Harkaways to a grand ball at the Palazzo Maraviglia. Midnight marauders, house-breaking, a mendicant friar and the brigands of the title soon follow. Hemyng writes rattling boys' adventure, and readers who enjoy Victorian tales of Greece, brigands and daring escapes will find this volume full of incident.
literary-character-of-men-of-genius-draw:
Isaac Disraeli draws these studies from writers' own confessions. His son, the Earl of Beaconsfield, edited this new edition. Frederick Warne published it in London in 1850. Disraeli's preface promises unity across his vernacular literature writings.

The pieces initiate readers into England's national literature, he claims. They also open a comprehensive view of human nature. Authors' faculties, tastes, fortunes, and feelings supply the evidence. Genius appears here through its own words rather than gossip. Gradations of faculties shape the portraits across the volume. Thinking materials, not literary topics alone, justify his collection.
murder-in-any-degree:
Owen Johnson gathers nine stories in this 1913 Century volume. Johnson had won fame with Stover at Yale and The Varmint. Two artists drew the pictures for the book. The title tale, Murder in Any Degree, leads the set.

Other tales include One Hundred in the Dark and A Comedy for Wives. The Lie, Even Threes, and Larry Moore fill out the list. Wedding gifts and a lottery bring lighter plots. Johnson writes of school, college, and married life with a shrewd eye. The set shows his range, from campus humor to darker tales of choice and chance.
nasa-tm-19710011740-a-specialized-model-:
S S Manson and C R Ensign of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a spring 1971 structures meeting in London. It offers a model for studying creep rupture data. Creep rupture is the slow failure of hot metal under steady load. Engineers need sound ways to stretch short test results into long service life forecasts.

Many rival time and heat formulas existed, with no agreed way to pick the best one. Manson's approach sidesteps that choice. Its general relation can contain all the common formulas at once. Each formula gets an equal chance to prove itself. The model defines its curves by values at chosen stations, not by fixed math forms.
north-of-fifty-three:
Bertrand W. Sinclair published North of Fifty-Three with Little, Brown in 1914, and Grosset and Dunlap reissued it in New York. Anton Otto Fischer drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows a woman gasping at gold. Sinclair had written The Land of Frozen Suns before this tale.

Chapter one introduces a lady and two gentlemen, the contents promise. Heart, hand, and pocketbook, then a will's bequest, stir the plot. Cariboo Meadows brings the northern gold country into view. A different sort of man, deep water, and the house that Jack built follow. Winter and a truce, the fires of spring, and the out trail close the listed chapters.
on-the-trail-of-grant-and-lee:
Frederick Trevor Hill wrote this joint study of Grant and Lee. The foreword recalls a taunt put to Minister Charles Adams. Adams replied that Confederate victories were won by fellow countrymen. Nearly fifty years had passed since that exchange, Hill notes. Local pride had twisted the Civil War story, he argues.

Hill urges North and South to share pride in American courage. Lincoln is now a national heritage, not a local hero, he says. Grant and Lee differed in views, tastes, and sympathies. Each still showed qualities that should make Americans proud. Hill places neither man on a pedestal. Their trials are followed as a very human story.
podcast-joerogan-0-Jalhl4CEE:
Andrew Wilson joins Joe Rogan for episode 2444 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Wilson is a debater known for sharp clashes on faith, morals, and the culture wars. His visits to big shows tend to spark heat.

Wilson and Rogan spar over the grounds of right and wrong and the place of God in them. Wilson holds a hard line and loves a clean win on points. Rogan tests him with the doubts his crowd sends in. Listeners who love a frank debate get one here at full length. The library keeps the episode as a record of the clash.
podcast-tuckercarlson-eRlkcRnC9eE:
Billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya joins Tucker Carlson to talk tech titans and a promised golden age under Trump. Chamath, a former Facebook leader turned venture capitalist, co-hosts the All-In podcast. He gives an insider's view of Zuckerberg, Rogan, and Musk and their place in the new order.

The two discuss how Silicon Valley's leaders shifted toward Trump and why. Chamath lays out his case that looser rules and new energy policy could spark a boom. Carlson tests the optimism against the fears of workers left behind before. Curious viewers get a rich insider's map of tech and power.
prisoners-of-chance-the-story-of-what-be:
Randall Parrish published a frontier romance with A. C. McClurg of Chicago in 1908, telling what befell Geoffrey Benteen, a borderman, through his love for a lady of France. Colour pictures by the Kinneys illustrate the book.

Opening chapters carry a request for aid, a risky venture, and a visit to a flag-ship, placing the hero between wilderness fighting and French colonial power. Parrish, known for tales of the old West and border wars, mixes battle, travel, and courtship. Readers get a fast story of loyalty and danger on an early American frontier.
recollections-and-letters-of-general-rob:
Captain Robert E. Lee, the general's son, wrote this life of his father from family memory and the general's own letters. Early chapters cover the elder Lee's service in the United States Army, his return from the Mexican War, and his years as head of West Point. He also helped suppress the John Brown raid at Harper's Ferry.

War chapters follow his choice to resign and lead the Virginia forces, his counsel to President Davis, and command of the Army of Northern Virginia. Letters to his wife and daughters run through accounts of Chancellorsville, Gettysburg, and the winter of 1863-4. The contents end with Cold Harbour and the siege of Petersburg.
scientific-american-volume-xxxvi-no-8-fe: Scientific American for February 24, 1877, is Volume XXXVI, Number 8, new series, priced at three dollars and twenty cents per annum with postage prepaid. Munn and Company, at Number 37 Park Row in New York, edit and own the weekly, founded in 1845; O. D. Munn and A. E. Beach are named on the masthead. Facing matter explains that the Supplement is a distinct paper, issued weekly with sixteen octavo pages and a handsome cover. Its own subscription runs five dollars a year, and single copies sell for ten cents.
soldiers-three: Rudyard Kipling heads a set of tales Soldiers Three, dated 1895, joined on the title page with The Story of the Gadsbys and In Black and White. The contents name The God from the Machine, Of Those Called, and Private Learoyd's Story. Later tales cover the Big Drunk Draf', the wreck of the Visigoth, the Solid Muldoon, and With the Main Guard. The first tale opens under a maxim of Private Mulvaney: hit a man and help a woman, and you cannot be far wrong.
stingaree:
E. W. Hornung wrote Stingaree, first copyrighted in 1905 and printed by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1910, with pictures by George W. Lambert. The book collects linked tales of an Australian bushranger who announces himself with the cry that gives him his name.

The opening chapters move from a voice in the wilderness to the black hole of Glenranald, then to a bushranger at bay. Hornung was known for tales of daring rogues. He sets the action in the bush country of Australia. There Stingaree's escapes, disguises, and cool manners turn crime stories into adventure. The touch stays light and wry throughout.
stories-of-inventors-the-adventures-of-i:
Russell Doubleday's Stories of Inventors, dated 1904, bears the subtitle The Adventures of Inventors and Engineers and promises true incidents and personal experiences. A frontispiece shows Marconi reading a message, setting the book's up-to-date tone.

The contents explain how Marconi telegraphs without wires, how Santos-Dumont flies his air-ship, how a fast train is run, and how automobiles work. Other chapters ride the fastest steamboats, visit life-savers and bridge builders, and look at submarines, long-distance telephony, moving pictures, a thinking typesetting machine, and making ice by heat. It is a tour of new machines told through the men who ran them.
story-hour-readers-book-three:
Ida Coe, an assistant principal in the New York City public schools, and Alice J. Christie, a primary teacher in the same system, prepared Story Hour Readers, Book Three, for the third year. It is a school reader built wholly from stories, poems, myths, and fables.

The contents open with Stevenson's The Land of Story Books. Hansel and Gretel and Longfellow's Hiawatha pieces follow. Then comes a run of Indian folklore. It holds The Beavers' Lodge, Manitou and the Squirrels, and Brother Rabbit. Greek tales of Diana and Apollo, Aesop's fables, northern folklore, and a Japanese hermit tale broaden the set. Short pieces and frequent changes keep young readers moving.
the-absentee: Maria Edgeworth wrote The Absentee, a novel. Its contents list a set of notes on the tale. Chapters numbered one through thirteen and beyond then follow. No chapter titles are given. The front notes explain two marks in the text. Notes from the print book sit in square brackets. The pound sign is written as the letter L.
the-apricot-tree:
A short tale for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, printed in London in 1851 and sold for twopence, opens on a fine autumn evening. The last sun rays fall through the window of a cottage standing in a pleasant lane a quarter mile from the village of Ryefield.

A narrow gravel walk leads to the cottage door between two small plots. On the right grow cabbages, onions, and other useful greens. On the left stand gooseberry and currant bushes, with one strip of flowers: stocks, sweet-peas, and rose-trees in full bloom over a neat quick-hedge. The neat, well-kept garden sets the scene for the moral tale the title promises.
the-bullitt-mission-to-russia-testimony-: The Bullitt Mission to Russia holds the testimony of William C. Bullitt before the Committee on Foreign Relations of the United States Senate, dated 1919. The list of heads starts with the committee meeting and Bullitt's official status. Ordered to Russia, the Council of Ten discussing Russia, and the troops at Archangel come next. What America wanted, the British terms, and the text of a projected peace proposal follow. Bullitt's report on Russia fills the next block, on its economic, social, and political state, with peace proposals and conclusions.
the-chief-legatee: Anna Katharine Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, wrote this mystery, copyrighted in 1906 and shown here in a special Weinstock, Lubin and Co. edition with water-color pictures by Frank T. Merrill. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. Part I is headed A Woman of Mystery, and its chapters open with a bride of five hours and a lady in number three.Nothing inside the book follows its front matter.
the-conflict-with-slavery-part-1-from-th: John Greenleaf Whittier's prose on slavery fills this volume, whose contents page runs from early pieces like Justice and Expediency and The Abolitionists. Later items treat Kansas, William Lloyd Garrison, and the election of 1872. Later sections turn to reform and politics, woman suffrage, Italian unity, and aid for the blind. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the essays themselves do not appear.
the-fruit-of-the-tree:
Edith Wharton wrote The Fruit of the Tree as a novel of mills and morals, printed at New York in 1907 with pictures by Alonzo Kimball. A hurt mill hand stands at the start.

In the surgical ward of Hope Hospital at Hanaford, a nurse bends over a young man whose right hand and arm lie bound in bandages. He asks if there is any show for him, meaning a chance to work again. Wharton sets a nurse's care, a mill owner's wealth, and a wife's cold rule in one frame, and asks what the rich owe to the folk their mills maim.
the-holly-tree:
The Holly-Tree, in three branches, is shown transcribed from the 1894 Chapman and Hall edition of Christmas Stories. No author is named in the pages present. The first branch, Myself, opens with a confession: the narrator has kept one secret in his life, and the secret is that he is a bashful man by nature.

That shyness, he says, explains countless places not visited and calls not made. His object is a plain account of being snowed up at the Holly-Tree Inn, a house of good entertainment for man and beast. The journey began in grief, after he parted forever from Angela Leath, who preferred his bosom friend Edwin, and resolved to sail for America.
the-life-of-the-bee:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote his famous essays on bees, and Alfred Sutro translated them for a New York edition of 1914, first published in May 1901. Contents run from the threshold of the hive through the swarm, young queens, the nuptial flight, and the massacre of the males. Chapter one opens with a disclaimer.

Maeterlinck says he offers no manual of bee keeping and no strict science monograph on bee species. Fine manuals already exist in France, England, and Germany, he notes. His book follows hive life as a drama of work, birth, flight, and death inside one small city.
the-portygee:
Joseph Crosby Lincoln's The Portygee opens on a raw December night at the South Harniss railway station. Clouds cloak the sky, pines thresh on the hilltops, and a wet, salty wind off the sea tears over dunes and frozen salt-meadows. It screams through the telegraph wires. The platform, in the narrator's judgment, is the lonesomest and most miserable spot imaginable: cold, dark, and forsaken.

At least, that is the opinion of the seventeen-year-old boy the down train has just deposited there, on time for once. Three other men share the platform: the station agent, Jim Young, who drives the depot wagon and whistles Silver Bells, and Doctor Holliday, the homeopath. Holliday is home from Boston and puffing a cigar. The boy looks out at black earth and sky beyond the station's kerosene gleam. He finds even the train's smelly warmth luxurious by comparison.
the-tale-of-buster-bumblebee: Arthur Scott Bailey's Slumber-Town tale of Buster Bumblebee was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1918, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title pages and publisher's lists are present in this record, placing the book among Bailey's Tuck-Me-In tales alongside Jolly Robin, Old Mr. Crow and Solomon Owl, Jasper Jay and Rusty Wren, and Daddy Longlegs and Kiddie Katydid, so Buster's own adventures do not appear.
the-world-set-free:
H. G. Wells wrote The World Set Free in 1913 and published it early in 1914. His preface calls it the latest of three fantasias of possibility. Each story imagines future developments of some contemporary force. Wells dedicates the book to Frederick Soddy's Interpretation of Radium. Long passages, he admits, owe much to that work's eleventh chapter. Chapters promise a new source of energy and a last war.

Wells says the story was written under the Great War's immediate shadow. Intelligent people everywhere felt disaster approaching in 1914. Few realized how near the crash already was. The novel famously imagines atomic bombs decades early. Its preface shows Wells thinking aloud about science and catastrophe.
